blocks.text: to learn with joy
Conditions for motivated learning
Motivation is everything that does our dog good.
Good motivation helps our dog to link behaviours with confidence and success.
Voice, touch, play and food are harmonious building blocks of motivation between us and our dog.
The right timing is decisive for successful motivation!
What is motivated is the mental connection to the handler in a successful situation while the desired behaviour patterns are present.
We set up the situation so that the dog is able to carry out the desired action and finally to be mentally with us.
Motivate from full inner conviction, be warm and affectionate.
Calm motivation for calm situations; emotional, intense motivation for letting loose.
Show your dog joy and appreciation wherever and whenever possible.
…definitely giving a good feeling
Observe the following during physical contact
Stroking is the warmest and most varied form of motivation.
Calm, slowly gliding strokes over the head and back calm the dog.
Calmly resting your hand on the dog for a longer time often works wonders and helps to build pauses and calm.
If the dog initially pulls away from the touch, stay relaxed and keep offering your hand. After a few days our dog will increasingly come to appreciate this gesture.
Physical gestures such as affectionate, conscious stroking through to playful patting on the shoulder or chest are part of daily communication.
Rule of thumb:
Stroke calmly to calm. Stroke motivatingly for action.
Stroke especially when the dog's attention is with you and it is looking at you, or when it is relaxed and composed.
…giving the highest motivation
Rules of play for hunting and prey drive
Play is a contest of strength, satisfaction of drives and emotion.
Use items that are easy to grip, such as bite rolls, knotted ropes or rope balls with a hand loop or pull cord.

Swap: with an inexperienced dog, keep a second toy ready so that it is not afraid of losing something when it comes to us. It will learn that it is worthwhile to come to us with the toy, in order to receive the other toy in exchange.

When the dog comes to you with the prey toy: praise it joyfully, stroke it if possible, and do not take the toy away immediately. Offer the second toy in a motivating way; it will usually drop the first toy.
In advanced training, giving up through alternative work: have the dog do "sit" or "down" and then swap for the second toy.
Tip: use a 3 – 4 metre long auxiliary line without a loop, so that you can call the dog to you in a supported, relaxed way if it runs off with the prey.
…really making a catch for once
Making a catch through food
Rewarding with food is the controlled variant of playful prey capture.
First let the dog perform the desired action and feed while it is still in the desired pattern.
Keep the food in a sturdy tin, which you only take out and open at the moment of confirmation.
Tip: carry the tin at chest height so that the dog learns to seek eye contact upwards towards you.
When opening the tin, speak in a mysterious, motivating and calm way to maintain the arc of suspense.
Timing and association
A dog associates a reward with the behaviour it is showing immediately. The time window for a reward is only a few seconds, and it must coincide exactly with the action to be rewarded.
If the reward comes late, the dog associates it with the behaviour it is showing at that moment, which, however, no longer corresponds to the behaviour that was to be rewarded.
A short marker word, always the same, can mark the moment of the correct behaviour precisely. The reward follows afterwards.

Mutual eye contact also has a physical effect. In a Japanese study (Nagasawa et al., 2015), the oxytocin levels of dogs and their owners rose after prolonged eye contact. Oxytocin is a hormone associated with bonding and well-being.
Eye contact between dog and you is therefore not only a training goal, but also strengthens the relationship.
Determining your dog's reward value
Whether something motivates is decided by the dog and not by the human.
The value of a reward depends on the situation: on distraction, hunger, tiredness, time of day, willingness to play and motivation.
The stronger the distraction, the higher the value of the reward must be.
Use food in small portions, but prefer motivating play, stroking and positive contact gestures.

Exercise: note down how successful treats, games, touches and forms of praise are. Observe how your dog reacts to them in a quiet environment, with moderate distraction and with strong distraction. Then arrange them in levels of success.
Record the result under “My reflection” at the end of this page. From it you can see which reward you use in which situation.
Changing the reward step by step
With a new behaviour, you initially reward every successful repetition so that the association is established securely.
Once the dog shows the behaviour reliably, you reward it less often and at irregular intervals. Irregular reward makes a behaviour more stable and less prone to disappearing again.
Increase difficulty, duration or distraction only one thing at a time, and only once the behaviour has succeeded several times in the easier situation.
In the event of a setback, go back one step and build up again from there.
Even when you reduce food, voice, touch and joy remain as recognition.
Source: Nagasawa M. et al. (2015): Oxytocin-gaze positive loop and the coevolution of human-dog bonds. Science 348 (6232), 333–336.
What you should definitely avoid
Avoid motivating a formally correct exercise when the dog is still strongly distracted mentally.
Avoid stroking while dogs are communicating tensely with each other (risk of provocation).
Avoid tug games before, during and after the time of tooth change. From the 8th month of life the teeth become increasingly firm. Then we can pull on the prey toy in a motivated way.
Avoid luring or persuading with food; food is the result, not the reason. There are exceptions. These should be made deliberately.
Avoid giving food when competitors are present (food envy).
Avoid brittle wooden sticks because of the potential risk of injury, and avoid games near sources of danger such as roads or drops.
Motivation is not a matter of the thinker, but of awareness.
Wrong motivation reinforces unwanted behaviour patterns.
Motivate your dog so as not to lose it.
